raw_text:
Cardiac contractility modulation (CCM) is an implantable device therapy for patients with heart failure (HF) who remain symptomatic despite guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT) and who are not optimal candidates for cardiac resynchronization therapy (CRT). Contemporary HF care has been transformed by neurohormonal antagonists, sodium–glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors, defibrillators, and CRT [1,2]. However, CRT benefits are largely confined to patients with electrical dyssynchrony, particularly wide QRS and left bundle branch block, whereas many patients with reduced or mildly reduced ejection fraction have narrow QRS complexes and persistent New York Heart Association (NYHA) class III symptoms [3,4]. Implantable cardioverter-defibrillators reduce sudden death but do not directly improve contractile function or symptoms [5]. CCM was developed to address this therapeutic gap.

CCM delivers relatively high-voltage, biphasic electrical signals to the right ventricular septum during the absolute refractory period. Because stimulation occurs after local depolarization, it does not trigger a new action potential or pace the ventricle; instead, it modifies cellular electrophysiology and contractile biology [6]. Early animal and isolated-muscle studies showed acute augmentation of contractility and intracellular calcium without conventional pacing capture [6–8]. Chronic canine HF models suggested favorable effects on left ventricular function and remodeling [9]. Importantly, mechanistic studies in patients and experimental systems indicate that CCM may improve calcium cycling, sarcoplasmic reticulum function, phosphorylation of contractile proteins, myocardial energetics, and maladaptive fetal-gene expression, rather than simply acting as a positive inotrope [10–12]. This distinction is clinically relevant because pharmacologic inotropes can increase oxygen demand and arrhythmic risk, whereas CCM has generally not shown a signal for excess arrhythmia in trials.

Clinical evidence has evolved from early feasibility work to randomized and registry studies. The FIX-HF-4 randomized double-blind crossover trial demonstrated improvements in exercise tolerance and health-related quality of life in symptomatic HF [13]. The larger FIX-HF-5 program tested CCM in patients with NYHA III–IV symptoms, reduced ejection fraction, and narrow QRS. Although the original trial did not meet its primary ventilatory anaerobic threshold endpoint, it improved peak oxygen consumption and Minnesota Living with Heart Failure Questionnaire scores, and predefined/post hoc analyses identified greater benefit in patients with ejection fraction at least 25% and NYHA class III symptoms [14–16]. Meta-analyses of randomized studies confirmed modest but consistent improvements in peak oxygen consumption, 6-minute walk distance, and quality of life, while remaining underpowered for mortality [17,18].

The pivotal FIX-HF-5C trial focused on the putative responder population: patients with LVEF 25%–45%, NYHA III or ambulatory IV symptoms, QRS <130 ms, and persistent symptoms despite GDMT [23]. CCM improved peak oxygen consumption, 6-minute walk distance, NYHA class, and quality-of-life scores, and reduced a short-term composite of cardiovascular death and HF hospitalization. Subsequent analyses and reviews have emphasized that CCM appears most useful as a symptom- and functional-capacity therapy rather than a proven mortality-reducing intervention [19,22,24]. The two-lead FIX-HF-5C2 system simplified implantation by eliminating the atrial sensing lead and demonstrated acceptable safety and performance, potentially broadening use in patients with atrial arrhythmias [25]. Observational data, including experience in permanent atrial fibrillation and the CCM-REG registry, support sustained improvements in functional status and fewer HF hospitalizations compared with pre-implant rates, though confounding remains unavoidable [20,21].

Patient selection is central. Current practice generally considers CCM for patients with LVEF 25%–45%, NYHA class III symptoms despite optimized therapy, sinus rhythm or controlled atrial arrhythmia depending on device generation, and no standard CRT indication. Patients with advanced frailty, frequent decompensation requiring inotropes, severe right ventricular failure, or limited life expectancy may derive less benefit. Implantation resembles pacemaker/defibrillator procedures and requires attention to septal lead positioning, sensing, interaction with ICDs, infection risk, and patient adherence to recharging [26]. Emerging work is assessing predictors of response, effects on myocardial strain, scar burden, HF with mildly reduced or preserved EF, and integration with contemporary quadruple GDMT [27–30].

In summary, CCM is a biologically plausible and increasingly evidence-supported therapy for a defined group of symptomatic HF patients with narrow QRS complexes who remain limited despite GDMT and lack a CRT indication. Its most reproducible benefits are improved symptoms, exercise capacity, and quality of life. Larger adequately powered studies are still needed to clarify effects on mortality, recurrent HF hospitalization, cost-effectiveness in modern care pathways, and optimal sequencing with other device-based HF therapies.
